questions.question: What does one BPE training step add to the learned vocabulary?
options: The least frequent whole word
The most frequent eligible adjacent symbol pair
Every character in the corpus again
A random embedding row
questions.explanation: BPE counts adjacent pairs in the current segmentation, selects the highest-frequency eligible pair, merges all matching occurrences, and records that merge in order.

questions.question: A pair appears 4 times in a word that occurs 3 times in the weighted corpus. How much does that word contribute to the pair count?
questions.explanation: Training counts corpus evidence, not distinct spellings. Four occurrences multiplied by a corpus frequency of three contribute twelve.

questions.question: Why are word-boundary markers or equivalent pre-tokenization boundaries important during training?
options: They make every word one token immediately
They prevent the trainer from accidentally treating unrelated cross-word pairs as ordinary within-word pairs
They remove the need for a vocabulary
They guarantee identical token counts in every language
questions.explanation: The boundary policy defines where pairs may form and lets the vocabulary distinguish a piece at a word ending from the same characters inside a word.

questions.question: What is the main risk of increasing the merge budget on a narrow domain-only corpus?
options: The tokenizer can memorize domain strings while fragmenting other traffic
The model no longer needs token IDs
All input becomes byte fallback
Training pair counts become negative
questions.explanation: More merges improve compression on observed strings, but a narrow sample can spend vocabulary capacity on domain-specific forms that transfer poorly.

questions.question: When encoding new text, in what order should learned merges be applied?
options: Alphabetically
From longest token to shortest token
In the rank order learned during training
In a new random order for each request
questions.explanation: The ordered merge table is the algorithm. Reordering merges can produce a different segmentation even when the vocabulary contains the same strings.

questions.question: A candidate tokenizer produces the same visible subword strings as production but assigns different token IDs. Is it compatible with the existing checkpoint?
options: Yes, because the strings look the same
Yes, if it is faster
No, because the IDs select different learned embedding rows
No, but only when the input contains spaces
questions.explanation: The checkpoint consumes integer IDs. A changed ID map can send the same-looking token to a different embedding and is therefore a hard contract break.

questions.question: Which evaluation best reveals whether a BPE vocabulary serves its real traffic?
options: Vocabulary size alone
Average compression on the training corpus alone
Token expansion, fallback, latency, and downstream quality broken down by protected traffic slices
The merge file's line count
questions.explanation: Averages hide weak languages, code styles, and domains. Slice-level token and downstream metrics show where the representation adds cost or loses useful structure.

questions.question: Which artifacts must remain versioned with the model checkpoint for a reproducible BPE release?
options: Only the vocabulary display name
Normalization, pre-tokenization, ordered merges, token-to-ID map, special tokens, and checkpoint
Only the source corpus size
Only the maximum request length
questions.explanation: Each listed artifact can change the IDs received by the model. They form one immutable encoding contract and must be tested and rolled back together.
